=== COLUMN 2 ===
Down Memory Lane in Stock Car Racing . . .
Al Kraure Collection
A full house and a full field of cars (top photo), two of the ingredients that go into the making of a
successful program by Promoter Tom Marchese, the fair park promoter. It was July of 1956 and Marshall
Teague was on the pole position. Troy Ruttman of Dearborn, Mich. (1956 Mercury), directly behind Teague,
came on to win the 150 mile race. The crowd totaled 30,718, the purse $22,475.
Roadster racing was the rage of race fans on the west coast in the 1930s. The lower photo is a lineup
shot taken at the Mines Field, Calif., Speedway in 1934. It was in this type of racing that the great Rex Mays
of Riverside, Calif., got his start in 1932. Mines Field was a road type course that also felt the bite of the racing
tires of the two-man cars used in those days.

Mario Andretti of Nazareth, Pa. (#11-1967 Ford) had nothing but trouble in the early laps of the July 9
200 mile stock car race here. First, the talented little Italian import spun in the south turn on the second mile.
Don White of Keokuk, Iowa (#2-1967 Dodge Charger), the eventual winner, barely slipped past Andretti's
errant mount. In the lower photo, Andretti gets his car back into traffic as J. C. Klotz of Fort Wayne, Ind.,
spins in the foreground. Others in the picture are: #55-Eddie Meyer; #4-Sal Tovella; #41-Bill Cheesbourg;
#97-Frank Freda and #8-Roger Regeth. Andretti later drove his way back into fourth place.

Scorers At Work
Charged with the responsibility of keeping the positions of the drivers in order at each major race at state
fair park is the crew of more than 50 trained scorers. Fred Williams and Christy Zwaagstra handle the scorers,
setting up their individual scoring charts and checking constantly with them as the race progresses. Each scorer
is assigned one of the cars in a race. As the car passes the scoring stand, the scorer checks the small timing
device and marks the total number of seconds it took the car to circle the track. On the next lap the timing
device then records the total elapsed time for the two laps. If the scorer misses his ( or her) assigned car on one
lap, the total elapsed time will indicate that there is a gap in the time. As each car comes around, the scorer
notes the total number of seconds and marks it in a space on the lap chart in front of him. Each scoring ehart
has the number of spaces to correspond with the number of miles in the race.
